To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we introduce a novel method for learning Bayesian networks, which (ii) reliably supports fast inference, by (iii) combining a heuristic structure learning method with a local search method, which (iv) improves the structure of a given BN, while (v) respecting a given treewidth constraint, (vi) by exploiting the recently developed connection between probabilistic inference and the satisfiability problem.

we introduce and study the problem of learning Bayesian networks with a treewidth and maximum state space size bound, and that we propose and evaluate methods that reliably solve the problem, which outperform state-of-the-art methods on a range of benchmarks.
(i) we introduce the first methods that learn fast inference BNs with respect to maximum state space size and (ii) we show that these methods produce BNs with superior inference performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of learning BNs that are suitable for fast probabilistic inference.
the question how to learn Bayesian networks that are fast in probabilistic reasoning.
learning fast-inference BNs that can be used for efficient probabilistic reasoning in a variety of real-world applications, such as medical diagnosis and decision making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method produces BNs with significantly faster exact probabilistc inference than BNs produced by state-of-the-art learning algorithms.
the proposed method is a promising alternative for learning Bayesian networks that support efficient inference.
the proposed methods for learning BNs are very effective for learning Bayesian Networks (BNs) which reliably support fast probabilistic inference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that it is possible to reliably learn BNs with fast inference.
our methods can learn BNs with significantly smaller state space size than the BNs that are learned with treewidth-based methods.

we show how to use the state-of-the-art MaxSAT-powered local search to learn BNs that support fast inference, and that this approach is more effective than using the treewidth measure for the same purpose.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the state space size of BNs is a more appropriate measure of their reasoning complexity than the treewidth measure, which has been the standard for decades.
BNs with larger treewidth can be more useful for fast inference than BNs with smaller treewidth.
the MaxSAT-powered local search method can reliably improve the inference complexity of BNs that are learned using a variety of different heuristics.
